findings.claim: Thomas Malthus is called "A Victorian economist (1766-1834)" in the <dfn> definition, in the glossary and on a flashcard.
findings.truth: Malthus died on 23 December 1834. Victoria came to the throne in June 1837, so he was never a Victorian. The definition prints the dates that contradict it. Corrected to "A British economist" in all three places.
findings.evidence: Malthus dates 1766-1834 given in the definition itself.

findings.claim: "Part (a) asks you to analyse language closely in the extract (AO1 + AO2)" and "This approach earns AO1 marks by linking context to the writer's purpose."
findings.truth: On the Edexcel 19th-century novel section part (a) is 20 marks under AO2 alone and part (b) is 20 marks under AO1 alone. AO3 (context) is not assessed on this section at all, so context earns no marks of its own. The sentence also carried a banned section code.

findings.claim: "Dickens opens the novella with a bold, conversational declaration: 'Old Marley was as dead as a doornail.'" Knowledge check 1 asks for the first line and marks that same option correct.
findings.truth: The first line is "Marley was dead: to begin with." The door-nail simile arrives five sentences later. The knowledge-check key marked the true answer (option 1) wrong; corrected to index 1, and the content now gives both lines in order.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave I, line 70 ("MARLEY was dead: to begin with.") and line 75-76 ("Old Marley was as dead as a door-nail.").

findings.claim: The <dfn> for "sibilance" defines it as "The repetition of the same consonant sound at the beginning of nearby words".
findings.truth: That is alliteration. Sibilance is the repetition of 's' sounds. The unit's own glossary already defines it correctly, so the tooltip contradicted the glossary.
findings.evidence: Standard literary terminology; glossary entry "sibilance" in the same lesson.

findings.claim: "Marley tells Scrooge that his own chain was 'as heavy and as long as this' seven years ago, and has grown since."
findings.truth: The Ghost says this of the chain SCROOGE already drags, not of Marley's: "Or would you know the weight and length of the strong coil you bear yourself? It was full as heavy and as long as this, seven Christmas Eves ago. You have laboured on it, since." The lesson reverses whose chain is being measured and loses the warning.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave I, lines 814-818.

findings.claim: "the fog is 'cold, bleak, biting,' and the weather is so severe that the city is wrapped in darkness".
findings.truth: Dickens writes "It was cold, bleak, biting weather". The quoted phrase describes the weather; the fog is a separate detail.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave I, line 161.

findings.claim: Fred's greeting is quoted as "Merry Christmas, uncle!"
findings.truth: The text reads "A merry Christmas, uncle! God save you!" The dropped article and capital M are small and the phrase is not on a memorisation card here, so it is recorded rather than edited.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave I, line 190.

findings.claim: The spirit's light "streamed from beneath it, in an unbroken flood upon the ground."
findings.truth: The text reads "which streamed from under it, in an unbroken flood upon the ground."
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave II, lines 1802-1805.

findings.claim: Students are told to zoom in on the phrase "golden idol".
findings.truth: Belle says "Another idol has displaced me" and, asked which idol, "A golden one." The welded phrase "golden idol" does not appear in the novella.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave II, Belle scene.

findings.claim: "If these shadows remain unaltered by the Future, I see a vacant chair ... and a crutch without an owner." Repeated on flashcard 10 as "A vacant chair...".
findings.truth: The Ghost says "I see a vacant seat, in the poor chimney-corner, and a crutch without an owner, carefully preserved. If these shadows remain unaltered by the Future, the child will die." The lesson changes "seat" to "chair" and moves the conditional to the front of the quotation.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave III, lines 2295-2298.

findings.claim: The <dfn> for "simile" opens "A comparison between two things without using 'like' or 'as'."
findings.truth: That is the definition of metaphor. A simile uses 'like' or 'as'. The tooltip then argued against its own first sentence.
findings.evidence: Standard literary terminology.

findings.claim: Withholding the dead man's identity is called "dramatic irony", defined as "where the audience or reader knows something that a character does not, OR where information is withheld to build tension."
findings.truth: The lesson itself says the reader "cannot be certain", so the reader knows no more than Scrooge: this is suspense. The definition had been widened until it no longer described dramatic irony, and that widened definition was also in the glossary. Both corrected; the <dfn> is kept.
findings.evidence: Stave IV withholds the name from reader and character alike until the gravestone.

findings.claim: "Most GCSE papers place the nineteenth-century novel in a closed book section ... Check your exam board's specimen paper for the exact mark allocation and timing."
findings.truth: This is a single-board unit and the allocation is known: 20 marks for each part, 80 marks for the paper, 2 hours 15 minutes, closed book. The hedge sent students away for a fact the lesson should state.

summary: Six HIGH findings: the Edexcel objectives are wrong wherever the unit states them - L1 exam tip, L7 Key Fact and L7 takeaway all give both parts AO1 + AO2 when part (a) is AO2 alone and part (b) is AO1 alone, and all three invite context that is not assessed on this section; an AQA-style rubric "You must refer to the context of the novel" sits on 14 practice questions; L2 names the wrong first line and its knowledge check marks the true first line wrong; and L2 gives Marley's chain the measurement Dickens applies to Scrooge's. Also "vacant chair" for "vacant seat", simile defined as metaphor, sibilance defined as alliteration, Malthus labelled Victorian though he died in 1834, and 56 banned "Level N" band names. The Stave 5 simile chain, "Darkness is cheap", Fan's death and Fred's "Christmas humour" line - the faults from the AQA sibling unit - do not recur here. Every other knowledge-check key and every match order is correct. No lesson is wholly clean because the practice-question faults are unit-wide; lesson 6 carries nothing else beyond a duplicate glossary entry.
